0.title: The Sound Church: Titus and the Gospel-Ordered Life
0.overview:
Titus is the most compressed of the three Pastoral Epistles — three chapters of extraordinary density that move from theology to character to conduct without pausing. Paul writes to Titus, his Greek co-worker and 'true child in a common faith,' whom he has left on Crete with a single, sprawling assignment: 'set in order what remains and appoint elders in every town' (1:5). The churches of Crete are young, disorganized, and under pressure from teachers who combine Jewish speculative traditions with moral permissiveness. Titus's task is to build a church that looks like the gospel it proclaims.

Crete was one of the ancient world's most storied islands — home to a hundred cities, to the legendary palace of Knossos and the Minoan civilization, and to a reputation for unreliability so notorious it had become proverbial in antiquity. The Cretan philosopher Epimenides (c. 6th century BC) had declared that 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons,' a statement Paul quotes in 1:12 without embarrassment — cultural honesty is not racism, and the false teachers have confirmed the description. Paul and Titus had apparently visited Crete together at some point unrecorded in Acts (probably during the period between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments), planted churches across the island, and then Paul left Titus to complete the work while he moved on.

The letter's organizing principle is the word 'sound' — hygiainō (healthy, health-giving). Sound doctrine (1:9; 2:1), sound faith (1:13; 2:2), sound speech (2:8) are the letter's repeated standard. The false teachers produce diseased teaching — teaching that makes people spiritually sick. Sound doctrine, by contrast, produces healthy congregations: older men of dignity, older women who form the younger, young people of self-control, slaves whose conduct adorns the gospel. The letter is a sustained argument that right belief and right living are inseparable — that the grace of God which saves also trains; that the gospel is not just good news about forgiveness but the power that produces a 'people for his own possession, eager for good works' (2:14).

Two Christological passages make Titus indispensable for preaching the full person of Christ. In 2:13 the Greek grammar (Sharp's Rule) identifies Jesus Christ as 'the great God and our Savior' — one of the New Testament's most explicit affirmations of full deity. In 3:4–7 the paragraph on regeneration, justification, and Spirit-renewal is one of the most complete soteriological statements in Paul's letters, anchoring the call to godly conduct in the deepest possible theological foundation: God saved us not because of what we did but entirely by his own mercy, through the Spirit's renewing, so that we might become heirs of the hope of eternal life. The letter that sounds like a manual of church order is, at its root, a profound meditation on grace.

1.title: The Ordered Church: Elders, Sound Doctrine, and False Teachers
1.overview:
The chapter moves through three phases: a greeting that frames the whole letter theologically (vv. 1–4), instructions for appointing elders (vv. 5–9), and a sharp confrontation with the false teachers already at work (vv. 10–16). The three phases are not disconnected: the qualifications for elders are defined precisely by the threat the false teachers represent, and the false teachers are exposed precisely by the standard the elders are meant to embody. The chapter is a study in contrast.

Paul opens with an unusually elaborate self-introduction — longer than any other Pauline greeting except Romans. 'Slave of God and apostle of Jesus Christ' — both titles together appear only here; in all other letters it is 'slave of Christ Jesus.' The 'slave of God' formulation links Paul to the great Old Testament prophets: Moses is called 'the servant of God' (Deut 34:5), as are the prophets generally (Amos 3:7). The letter is situating Paul within the long prophetic tradition of commissioned spokesmen who did not choose their message. He is a servant, not an entrepreneur.

The Cretan churches face a specific combination of error: Judaizing pressure ('especially those of the circumcision party,' v. 10) combined with moral disorder. The teachers talk about the law but their lives disprove their doctrine. Paul's diagnostic is devastating: 'To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works' (vv. 15–16). The corruption is not principally intellectual but moral; the false teachers' theology serves their lifestyle.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ, for the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth 'which accords with godliness' (v.1) — in hope of eternal life, promised before the ages began by the God who never lies (v.2), and manifested at the proper time in the preaching entrusted to him by the command of God our Saviour (v.3). To Titus, his true child in a common faith: grace and peace (v.4).
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Cannot Lie, Writing to Crete

Apseudes — the unlying God — occurs only here in the New Testament, and its placing is deliberate. This letter is going to an island whose most famous literary export is the line quoted in verse 12: Cretans are always liars. The Greeks even had a verb for it. The first thing Paul says about God, writing to a place proverbial for deceit, is that he cannot lie.

Note also the chain in verses 2-3: an eternal promise made before the ages began, manifested at an appointed hour, and then entrusted to a man to announce — the deposit word again. That is how the truth reaches anybody, which is why appointing the right men in every town is not administration but the survival of the thing itself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Titus is a more formidable figure than his one short letter suggests. A Greek and uncircumcised, he was taken by Paul to the Jerusalem council as a living test case, and Paul records with satisfaction that he was not compelled to be circumcised (Gal 2:1-3) — Titus was the exhibit in the argument that settled whether Gentiles could be Christians without becoming Jews. He was also sent into the worst of the Corinthian crisis, and his return with good news comforted Paul (2 Cor 7:6, 13-15). Where Timothy is timid and needs steadying, Titus gets the hard postings.

Now: The definition in verse 1 is the test that governs all three of these letters: knowledge of the truth 'which accords with godliness'. Truth is recognised by the life it produces, and a knowledge that leaves a man unchanged has failed the definition whatever its content. Watch too the title 'Saviour', applied to God in verse 3 and to Christ in verse 4, and alternating six times in three chapters. The interchange is not careless; it is the argument Paul will make explicit at 2:13.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the longest opening sentence in any of Paul's short letters, and the length is the point. Titus is going to face people on Crete who claim superior knowledge, and Paul sets out in three verses where the truth actually comes from.

'A servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ.' The combination appears nowhere else in Paul. Elsewhere he is a slave of Christ Jesus; here he is God's slave and Christ's apostle, and the pairing is deliberate in a letter that will call both Father and Son 'our Saviour' within four verses.

Then the purpose: 'for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness.' There is the test that runs through all three of these letters. Truth is recognised by the life it produces. A knowledge that leaves a man unchanged has failed the definition, whatever its content.

'In hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began.'

The phrase is apseudes — the unlying God, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. Now recall where this letter is going. Crete, whose most famous literary export was the line Paul quotes in verse 12: Cretans are always liars. The first thing he says about God, in a letter to an island proverbial for deceit, is that he cannot lie.

'Before the ages began' is the same phrase as 2 Timothy 1:9 — the promise was made before there was anyone to make it to. Then verse 3: 'at the proper time manifested in his word.' The eternal purpose stayed hidden until an appointed moment, and then came out into the open.

And notice the last link in the chain: manifested 'through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Saviour.' The deposit word again. An eternal promise, revealed at the right hour, and then handed to a man to announce. That is how it reaches anybody — which is why appointing the right men in every town, in the very next verse, is not administration but the survival of the thing.

verseByVerse.quote: To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'To Titus, my true child in a common faith.' The same phrase used of Timothy (1 Tim 1:2) — genuine, legitimate, the real article. Titus was almost certainly converted under Paul.

And he is a more formidable figure than his single short letter suggests. He was a Greek, and uncircumcised, and Paul took him to the Jerusalem council as a living test case — and records with some satisfaction that he was not forced to be circumcised (Gal 2:1-3). Titus was the exhibit in the argument that settled whether Gentiles could be Christians without becoming Jews.

He was also the man Paul sent into the worst of the Corinthian crisis, and whose return with good news comforted him (2 Cor 7:6, 13-15). Where Timothy is timid and needs steadying, Titus gets the hard postings. Paul has now left him on Crete.

'In a common faith' — the word means shared, held in partnership. It is a small thing and worth noticing: the apostle and his delegate are not on different tiers of Christianity. They hold the same faith on the same terms.

Then the greeting, and there is a difference from both letters to Timothy. There Paul wrote 'grace, mercy and peace'; here, as to churches, it is simply 'grace and peace.' Whatever the reason, the tone matches everything else we know: this is a letter to a man who does not need to be handled gently.

'From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.' Watch this title through the letter. Paul applies 'Saviour' to God in verse 3 and to Christ here, and he will keep alternating — God our Saviour, Christ our Saviour, six times in three chapters. The interchange is not careless. It is the same argument he will make explicit at 2:13.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Appointing Elders in Every Town
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul left Titus on Crete to put what remained in order and appoint elders in every town (v.5): men above reproach, husbands of one wife, whose children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination (v.6). For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach — not arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent, or greedy for gain (v.7), but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined (v.8) — holding firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so as to instruct in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it (v.9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder and Overseer Are One Office

Paul says 'elders' in verse 6 and 'overseer' in verse 7 inside a single sentence about a single group of men. It is one of the clearest indications in the New Testament that the two terms describe the same office — presbyteros naming the man and episkopos his function. Note too that the elders are plural in each town: Paul's answer to disorder is not a stronger central figure but properly constituted local leadership, which means Titus's job is to work himself out of one.

'God's steward' is oikonomos, the household manager — very often a trusted slave — who ran the estate on the owner's behalf. The title carries real authority and no ownership whatever. He spends another man's money and answers for it.

And observe the proportion: eleven items of character, then one competence. That single competence has two halves which must be kept together — to instruct and to rebuke. A man who can only encourage will watch the flock be eaten; a man who can only refute will do the eating himself.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 5 is honest about the state Paul left things in — 'what remained' concedes the work was unfinished, and 'put into order' is used of setting a broken bone or refitting a ship. Crete was an island Homer credited with a hundred cities, and the congregations existed without being in working condition.

Now: The hardest line is that an elder's children are 'believers', which is higher than 1 Timothy 3's requirement that he keep them submissive, and it has troubled sensitive men ever since, since no father can produce faith in a child. Two things keep it from crushing anybody: the Greek word can mean faithful or trustworthy as well as believing, and the qualifying clause names the actual concern — debauchery and insubordination, wild living and rebellion. The question is not whether a man has guaranteed his children's salvation but whether his household is visibly out of control. On a new mission field, the practical sense is plain: a man whose own family has not been persuaded is not the man to persuade a town.

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'This is why I left you in Crete.' Not abandoned — the verb is a deliberate posting. And what he was left to do has two parts: 'put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town.'

'What remained' concedes that the work was unfinished, and 'put into order' is a word used of setting a broken bone or refitting a ship. Paul is honest that he left a mess behind. The churches on Crete existed and were not yet in working condition.

'Elders in every town.' Not one central church but congregations scattered across an island Homer credited with a hundred cities. And the plural is standard: elders, in each place. Paul's answer to disorder is not a stronger central figure but properly constituted local leadership — which is why Titus's job is to work himself out of one.

Then the qualifications, and they run closely parallel to 1 Timothy 3 with one striking difference. 'Above reproach' heads the list again — nothing outstanding that anyone can lay hold of. 'The husband of one wife' — a one-woman man, the same phrase, and it means faithfulness rather than a ruling on remarriage.

The difference is the children. In 1 Timothy an overseer must manage his household well and keep his children submissive; here 'his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.' That is a considerably higher bar, and it has troubled sensitive men ever since, since no father can produce faith in a child.

Two things keep it from crushing anybody. The Greek word can mean faithful or trustworthy as well as believing, and the qualifying clause that follows explains the concern — debauchery and insubordination, wild living and rebellion. The question is not whether a man has guaranteed his children's salvation but whether his household is visibly out of control. And on a new mission field with a first generation of converts, the practical sense is plain: a man whose own family has not been persuaded is not the man to persuade a town.

verseByVerse.quote: For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now switches terms — 'elder' in verse 6, 'overseer' in verse 7 — and the switch is worth registering, because it is one of the clearest indications in the New Testament that the two words describe the same office. He is in the middle of one sentence about one set of men.

'As God's steward.' The oikonomos was the household manager, very often a trusted slave, who ran the estate on the owner's behalf. The title carries real authority and no ownership whatever. He spends another man's money and answers for it.

Then five things he must not be, and they read like a portrait of a bad manager. 'Arrogant' is literally self-pleasing — the man who suits himself. 'Quick-tempered' — prone to anger. 'A drunkard' and 'violent' — the latter meaning a striker, a man who hits people. And 'greedy for gain', which on Crete was the live issue: the false teachers were in it for shameful gain (v.11), and a man who wants money should not be given charge of a church's.

Then six he must be. 'Hospitable' — literally a lover of strangers, and in a world without inns worth staying in, the church ran on it. 'A lover of good'. 'Self-controlled', 'upright', 'holy', and 'disciplined' — a man with a grip on himself.

Notice that all eleven items are about character, and then verse 9 gives the single competence: 'He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught.' Hold firm — cling to; and 'as taught', meaning as it was handed to him rather than as he has developed it.

And the purpose has two halves that must be kept together: 'so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.' Building up and pulling down. A man who can only encourage will watch the flock be eaten; a man who can only refute will do the eating himself. Paul requires both.

Which is why the character list comes first and is eleven times longer. The one skill demanded is inseparable from the man exercising it, and on an island of empty talkers (v.10) the difference between a true elder and a false teacher was never going to be fluency.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There are many insubordinate empty talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision party (v.10). They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole households by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not (v.11). A Cretan prophet of their own said, 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons' (v.12) — and the testimony is true, so Titus is to rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith (v.13), not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn from the truth (v.14). To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled nothing is, and both their minds and consciences are defiled (v.15). They profess to know God but deny him by their works, being detestable, disobedient and unfit for any good work (v.16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Quoting a Pagan, and Agreeing With Him

The line in verse 12 is attributed to Epimenides of Knossos, a Cretan seer of the sixth century BC — and Paul does this elsewhere, quoting Aratus at Athens (Acts 17:28) and Menander to Corinth (1 Cor 15:33). The reputation was proverbial: the Greeks had a verb, kretizein, 'to Cretanise', meaning to lie.

Then Paul says flatly, 'This testimony is true' — an apostle endorsing a pagan poet's national slur, in Scripture. Two things keep it from being what it looks like. He is not making a racial claim: he has just left elders and congregations on Crete and Titus is to build them up. What he affirms is that the island's own moral self-assessment was accurate and that these particular teachers are living down to it. And the purpose clause changes everything — rebuke them sharply that they may be sound in the faith. The sharpness aims at their health; sound is the medical word. A rebuke meant to make someone well is a different act from one meant to put them in their place, even when the words are identical.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: 'They must be silenced' means to muzzle, to stop the mouth — the word for putting a bit in a horse's mouth. That sits alongside the gentleness Paul commands elsewhere (2 Tim 2:25), and the two are not in conflict once the distinction is seen: gentleness governs how you treat the deceived; silencing is for those doing the deceiving, when whole households are being overturned while the discussion continues. And the motive is named — 'shameful gain', the same disqualification listed for an elder nine words earlier in verse 7.

Now: Verse 15 is easily misused. 'To the pure all things are pure' is a genuine principle against food laws and ritual restriction, standing with 1 Tim 4:4 and the Lord's own verdict in Mark 7:15-19. But Paul is talking about things — food, days, created stuff — not about actions. The verse abolishes ritual defilement; it does not abolish sin. And note the terrible logic of the second half: when both mind and conscience are stained, no internal instrument is left to detect the problem, which is precisely why such men are confident and why they must be silenced rather than reasoned with. Verse 16 then names the shape of it: profession with the mouth, denial by the works — the same figure as 2 Tim 3:5, and the hardest person a church has to deal with, because an open opponent can be answered and he is usually inside.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers.' The 'for' ties this straight to the elder qualifications: this is why Titus needs men who can rebuke. And 'many' is not encouraging. The problem on Crete was not a fringe.

Three words describe them. 'Insubordinate' — the same word used of an elder's children in verse 6, unruly, refusing to be under anything. 'Empty talkers' — literally vain-speakers, men whose words carry nothing. And 'deceivers', mind-misleaders.

'Especially those of the circumcision party.' The same trouble as in Galatia — Jewish Christians pressing the law on Gentile converts. Titus of all people knew what was at stake, having been the test case at Jerusalem (Gal 2:3).

Then verse 11, and Paul is unusually blunt: 'They must be silenced.' The word means to stop the mouth, to muzzle; it is used of putting a bit in a horse's mouth. Not engaged in extended dialogue. Stopped.

That sits alongside the gentleness Paul commands elsewhere — correcting opponents with gentleness (2 Tim 2:25) — and the two are not in conflict once you see what he distinguishes. Gentleness governs how you treat the deceived. Silencing is for those doing the deceiving, when a congregation is being destroyed while the discussion continues.

And the reason is given in two parts. First: 'they are upsetting whole families.' The verb means to overturn, and the object is not individuals but households — which on Crete were the churches. Whole congregations were being turned over at once.

Second: 'by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.' There it is again, as in every one of these letters. Money is underneath the false teaching. And 'shameful' is Paul's own verdict on it — the same disqualification he had just listed for an elder in verse 7. The contrast is exact: the man who must not be greedy for gain, set against the men who teach for it.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons."'

Paul is quoting a pagan. The line is attributed to Epimenides of Knossos, a Cretan seer of the sixth century BC, whom the Greeks regarded highly enough that Paul can call him a prophet without irony being the whole point. He does the same elsewhere — quoting Aratus at Athens (Acts 17:28) and Menander to the Corinthians (1 Cor 15:33).

The reputation was real and proverbial. The Greeks had a verb, kretizein, 'to Cretanise', meaning to lie. Crete's boast that it held the tomb of Zeus was, to other Greeks, the founding Cretan falsehood, since Zeus could not die.

Then Paul says, flatly: 'This testimony is true.' An apostle endorses a pagan poet's national slur, in a letter of Scripture. It needs care.

Two things keep it from being what it looks like. First, Paul is not making a racial claim about Cretans as such — he has just left elders and congregations there, and Titus is to build them up. What he affirms is that the island's own moral self-assessment was accurate, and that the false teachers he has just described are living down to it. A Cretan said this about Crete; Paul agrees that the cap fits the men in question.

Second, note the purpose clause, because it changes everything: 'Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith.'

The sharpness has an aim, and the aim is their health. Sound is the medical word — Paul wants these people well. A rebuke intended to make somebody healthy is a different act from a rebuke intended to put them in their place, even when the words are identical. And the word for sharply means severely, cuttingly; a surgeon's severity is not cruelty.

The pastoral judgement underneath is that different people need different treatment. Timothy, timid, was told to be gentle and patient. Titus, on Crete, is told to cut. Paul has no single register, and a minister who only ever has one has not learned from him.

verseByVerse.quote: not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth.' The same material as at Ephesus — myths and endless genealogies (1 Tim 1:4) — and note the two halves: speculation on one side, and man-made commands on the other. Fantasy and legalism, which look like opposites and regularly arrive together.

Then verse 15, which is easily misused: 'To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.'

The first half is a genuine principle and Paul means it. Against teachers imposing food laws and ritual restrictions, he says that for a person made clean by God, created things are clean. It is the same argument as 1 Timothy 4:4 — everything created by God is good — and behind both stands the Lord's own verdict, that nothing entering a man from outside defiles him (Mark 7:15-19).

What it does not mean is that a pure person may do anything he likes, or that morality is decided by the state of the doer. Paul is talking about things — food, days, created stuff — not about actions. The verse abolishes ritual defilement; it does not abolish sin.

The second half is the sharper observation: 'to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.' Defilement is not in the object but in the eye. A corrupted mind manages to corrupt whatever it handles, including good and innocent things — and the reverse of the first principle is that such a man cannot be cleaned by rules about food, because the trouble is not in the food.

'Both their minds and their consciences are defiled.' Two faculties, and between them a man is finished. The mind judges what is true; the conscience judges what is right. When both are stained there is no internal instrument left to detect the problem — which is precisely why such men are confident, and why they must be silenced rather than reasoned with.

verseByVerse.quote: They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works.'

It is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, and it names the exact shape of the error. These men are not atheists and would be insulted to be called unbelievers. They profess — they make the claim, publicly and probably loudly. What they deny is denied by their works.

The two verbs are set against each other deliberately. Confession and denial are the great pair in the New Testament — whoever confesses me before men, and whoever denies me (Matt 10:32-33). Paul says a man can perform the first with his mouth while performing the second with his life, and that the second is the one that counts.

This is the same figure as 2 Timothy 3:5 — having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. The letters keep returning to him, because he is the hardest person a church has to deal with. An open opponent can be answered; a man whose profession is orthodox and whose life contradicts it cannot be, and he is usually inside.

Three words follow, and they escalate. 'Detestable' — the word is used in the Greek Old Testament of idols and unclean things, an abomination. Men who talk endlessly about purity are pronounced unclean. 'Disobedient' — the same root as the insubordination of verse 10.

And then: 'unfit for any good work.' The word is adokimos, the assayer's term for metal tested and rejected. It closes the chapter on the note that opened it — a knowledge of the truth which accords with godliness (v.1). Here is knowledge that accords with nothing.

'Good works' will now dominate the rest of the letter. Titus contains the phrase six times in three short chapters — more densely than anything else Paul wrote — and it starts here, with men who are fit for none. Paul is not about to argue that works save; he will say the opposite as plainly as it can be said (3:5). He is going to argue that grace produces them, and that a profession which produces none has already been assayed and failed.

2.title: Adorning the Doctrine: The Gospel-Shaped Community
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the great household-code passage of Titus, but its organizing principle is not the household as such — it is the gospel. Each group is given specific instruction (older men, older women, young women, young men, slaves) and each instruction is bracketed by a purpose clause pointing back to the gospel: 'so that the word of God may not be reviled' (v. 5); 'so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us' (v. 8); 'so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior' (v. 10). The conduct of ordinary Christians in ordinary roles is itself a form of gospel proclamation.

The chapter's theological center is vv. 11–14, one of the densest Christological paragraphs in the New Testament. Paul describes the 'appearing' (Greek: epiphaneia) of God's grace in the incarnation (v. 11) and the 'appearing' of Christ at his return (v. 13) as the two temporal anchors of Christian existence. Between the first appearing and the second, the grace of God is 'training' the church — actively discipling every believer toward godliness. The chapter that begins with practical ethics ends with the deepest possible theological grounding: the grace that saves is also the grace that trains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — What Accords With Sound Doctrine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine (v.1). Older men: sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, love and steadfastness (v.2). Older women: reverent, not slanderers or slaves to much wine, teachers of what is good (v.3), so training the young women to love husbands and children (v.4), to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled (v.5). Younger men: self-controlled (v.6).

Titus himself is to be a model of good works, showing integrity and dignity in his teaching (v.7), with sound speech beyond condemnation, so that an opponent is put to shame with nothing evil to say (v.8). Bondservants are to be submissive, well-pleasing, not argumentative (v.9), not pilfering but wholly trustworthy, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Doctrine Has a Shape

Verse 1 is precise: Titus is not told to teach sound doctrine, which he must obviously do, but to teach what accords with it — what befits it, its natural clothing. That is why ten verses follow with no theology expounded at all, only how various people are to behave. Doctrine has a shape, and a life either fits it or does not.

The chapter's key word is sophron — sound-minded, self-controlled — which appears five times in fifteen verses and is plainly Paul's central concern for Crete. Every group gets it.

And the climax is verse 10's kosmeo, to arrange or beautify, the root behind 'cosmetic' — used of setting a jewel so the stone shows to best advantage. Paul tells slaves, people with no legal standing whose testimony was inadmissible in court, that their honesty in small things displays the doctrine of God to its best advantage. The gospel commends itself not chiefly by argument or spectacle but by the ordinary reliability of people with nothing to gain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verses 4-5 give modern readers most trouble and repay exact reading. 'Working at home' is one word meaning a home-worker, and in the first century the household was a productive economic unit — weaving, food, managing slaves and accounts — so a competent wife ran a small business; Proverbs 31 describes such a woman, and she buys fields and trades. 'Submissive to their own husbands' has a qualifier that is regularly dropped: this is about a marriage, not women as a class under men as a class, and it sits within a frame that tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her (Eph 5:25). And the only reason Paul gives is missionary: 'that the word of God may not be reviled.' A movement whose converts were seen to wreck households would have been dismissed unheard.

Now: Note who does the teaching in verse 4. The older women train the younger — the instruction bypasses Titus, the minister on the island, entirely. And note that loving husband and children is something taught: Paul does not assume affection arrives automatically with marriage and motherhood, or that a woman struggling there is defective. It is learned, from someone further along. Note also that Paul makes teaching a requirement for older women in the same breath in which he elsewhere restricts authoritative teaching over men in the assembly (1 Tim 2:12) — whatever that passage means, it cannot mean women do not teach, since the man who wrote it commands them to.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'But as for you' — the contrast with the empty talkers who have just been described as unfit for any good work. Against them, Titus, and a single instruction: 'teach what accords with sound doctrine.'

Notice the phrasing, because it is doing something precise. Titus is not told to teach sound doctrine, which he must obviously do, but to teach what fits it — what befits, what is appropriate to it. The whole chapter is about behaviour, and Paul introduces it as the natural clothing of a body of truth.

That is the letter's governing conviction. Doctrine has a shape, and a life either fits it or does not. And it explains why what follows is so ordinary: no theology is expounded for ten verses, only how various people are to conduct themselves — because that is what accords with the theology.

'Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled.' Paul begins with the group most likely to think itself exempt. These are not officers; they are simply the older men in the congregation, and they get instructions like everybody else.

'Sober-minded' is the clear-headed word again; 'dignified' means worthy of respect; 'self-controlled' is sophron, sound-minded, which will appear five times in this short chapter and is plainly Paul's central concern for Crete.

Then three more: 'sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.' The medical word attaches here not to doctrine but to graces — healthy faith, healthy love, healthy endurance. And the third is the one that belongs particularly to age. Faith and love are asked of everyone; hypomone, staying under the weight, is what a long life is uniquely placed to have learned and uniquely tempted to abandon at the end.

There is a quiet dignity in this. Paul does not write old men off or reduce them to recipients of care. He gives them a standard to meet, which is a form of respect.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Older women likewise' — the same word, the same expectation. Paul is working through the congregation by age and sex, and nobody is left out.

'Reverent in behaviour.' The adjective is striking: it is a temple word, meaning fitting for holy things, as a priestess carries herself in a sacred place. Paul is saying that an older Christian woman should move through ordinary life as though it were holy ground — which, given what he has just said about doctrine having a shape, it is.

Then two things they are not to be, and they are startlingly specific. 'Not slanderers' — the word is diabolos, the same term used of the devil himself, meaning an accuser, a thrower-across. That is a heavy word to use of gossip, and Paul uses it deliberately: a tongue that circulates accusations is doing recognisably the devil's own work.

'Or slaves to much wine.' The phrase is blunt and it names a real problem — enslaved to it. Paul does not treat this as unmentionable or beneath discussion, and the candour is itself pastoral. Congregations that cannot name such things cannot help anyone caught in them.

These two are not a random pair. They are the characteristic temptations of people with time on their hands and less to occupy them than they once had — which is why the positive instruction follows immediately.

'They are to teach what is good.' One word in Greek, and it occurs nowhere else in the Bible: teachers-of-good. Here is the answer to the two vices. An older woman with an empty diary will either fill it with wine and other people's business or with this, and Paul assigns her a job.

And it should be said plainly what the job is not. Paul restricted women from teaching authoritatively over men in the assembly (1 Tim 2:12), and here in the same breath he makes teaching a requirement for older women. Whatever the first passage means, it cannot mean women do not teach, because the man who wrote it commands them to.

verseByVerse.quote: and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The content of that teaching is now specified, and this is the passage that gives modern readers most trouble. It repays reading exactly.

'And so train the young women.' The verb means to bring to their senses, to school in sound-mindedness — the sophron root again. And note the mechanism Paul has set up: the older women teach the younger. Not Titus. He is the minister on the island and this instruction bypasses him entirely, handing the formation of young wives to older women who know what they are talking about.

'To love their husbands and children.' Two more single Greek words — husband-lovers and child-lovers — and it is worth noticing that these are taught. Paul does not assume affection arrives automatically with marriage and motherhood, or that a woman struggling there is defective. It is something learned, from someone further along.

Then: 'self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands.'

'Working at home' is one word, meaning a worker at home or a home-keeper. In the first century the household was a productive economic unit — weaving, food, managing slaves and accounts — and a competent wife ran a small business. Proverbs 31 describes exactly such a woman, and she buys fields and trades. The word is about diligence and industry in the sphere she had, not a rule confining every Christian woman in every century to the house.

'Submissive to their own husbands.' The qualifier matters and is regularly dropped. Paul is not describing women as a class under men as a class; he is speaking of a marriage. And it stands within a New Testament frame that tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her (Eph 5:25) — a demand which, if anything, costs more.

Then the reason, and it is the only one given: 'that the word of God may not be reviled.' This is missionary strategy, not metaphysics. Paul's concern throughout is how the gospel looks to a watching pagan society. A movement whose converts were seen to wreck households would have been dismissed unheard, and he will not have the message discredited by the messengers' domestic chaos.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled.' One instruction, and it is the same word again — sophron, sound-minded. Every group in this chapter gets it, but for young men it is the only thing said.

The brevity is its own comment. Paul has three words for the group most likely to think itself the exception, and he does not elaborate.

Then Titus himself, who is a young man too, and the instruction turns personal. 'Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works.' The word for model is typos — a die, a stamp, the pattern that shapes what is pressed against it. Titus is not merely to teach the chapter; he is to be the mould it is struck from.

'In your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned.' Integrity here means uncorruptedness — teaching with no self-interest mixed in, which on an island of men teaching for shameful gain (1:11) was the visible difference. And 'sound speech that cannot be condemned' does not mean speech nobody dislikes; it means speech that gives no legitimate handle.

Which is exactly the purpose clause: 'so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.'

Paul assumes there will be opponents; he does not aim at being liked. What he aims at is that when the opposition comes, it should have nothing true to work with. There is a great difference between a church that is attacked and a church that has handed its attackers the ammunition, and only the second is a disgrace.

Note also 'about us'. Paul includes himself. What a young minister on Crete does with his teaching and his conduct will be laid at the door of the whole enterprise, the apostle included — which is a considerable weight to put on a man, and Paul puts it.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last group, and the largest in that world. 'Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything.'

As at 1 Timothy 6:1-2, this must be read for what it does and does not do. Paul is not endorsing the institution — he lists slave-traders among the lawless (1 Tim 1:10), tells masters they answer to a Master who shows no partiality (Col 4:1), tells a slave to take freedom if he can get it (1 Cor 7:21), and sends a runaway back as a beloved brother (Philem 16). What he is doing here is telling people with no legal power how to live with dignity inside a system they cannot change.

Four instructions follow, and they are concrete. 'Well-pleasing' — giving satisfaction. 'Not argumentative' — not answering back, the constant low-level resistance of the powerless. 'Not pilfering' — and the word means petty theft, helping yourself in small ways, which was so universal among slaves that nobody thought it stealing. Paul does.

'But showing all good faith' — complete trustworthiness. Taken together, the picture is a slave whose owner discovers that things stopped going missing and the back-answering stopped, and cannot account for it.

Then the reason, and it is one of the most dignifying sentences in the New Testament: 'so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour.'

The verb is kosmeo — to arrange, to beautify, the root behind 'cosmetic'. It is used of setting jewels so that the stone shows to best advantage. Paul tells slaves — people with no legal standing, whose testimony was inadmissible in court, who could be beaten at will — that their honesty in small things displays the doctrine of God to its best advantage.

Consider what that means for how the gospel commends itself. Not chiefly by argument or spectacle, but by the ordinary reliability of people with nothing to gain. The most powerless people in Crete are told they are the setting in which the jewel is shown, and everything in this chapter has been building to it: doctrine has a shape, and a life either fits it or does not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people (v.11), training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in the present age (v.12), waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ (v.13) — who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works (v.14). Titus is to declare these things and to exhort and rebuke with all authority, letting no one disregard him (v.15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Our Great God and Saviour Jesus Christ

Verse 13 is among the most important Christological texts in the New Testament. Is Paul naming one person or two — 'our great God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ', or 'our great God and Saviour, who is Jesus Christ'? The Greek settles it: a single definite article governs both nouns, joined by kai, with a personal name attached — the construction described by Granville Sharp, under which two singular personal nouns joined this way refer to one person. So Jesus Christ is called, straightforwardly, our great God — one of a small handful of places where the New Testament applies the word to him without qualification (cf. John 1:1; 20:28; Rom 9:5; 2 Pet 1:1, which has the identical construction).

This also explains the alternation running through the letter. Paul says God our Saviour and Christ our Saviour, back and forth, six times in three chapters (1:3, 1:4, 2:10, 2:13, 3:4, 3:6). It looks careless. It was an argument being assembled, and here it closes — which means the slave not pilfering in a Cretan kitchen is adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v.10), and the God in question is the man who died for him (v.14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The 'for' at the head of verse 11 is the hinge of the chapter. Ten verses of household instruction, and then the reason underneath all of it — this great passage exists to explain why an older woman should not gossip and a slave should not pilfer. And the order is never reversed in Paul: not behave well so that grace may appear, but behave well because it already has. Note too what 'all people' means in context — Paul has just addressed old men, old women, young women, young men and slaves. All kinds of people, which on an island offering graded religion and inner knowledge is the point.

Now: The astonishment of verse 12 is that grace is the subject of the training verb — paideuo, the schooling and discipline of a child. Grace is not merely what pardons ungodliness; grace is the schoolmaster. Anyone who has been told that too much emphasis on grace produces loose living should sit with this: Paul's answer is not that grace must be balanced by law, but that grace itself does the teaching, and does it better, because law can restrain conduct and cannot reach the wanting. The three adverbs then face three directions — sound-minded toward yourself, upright toward others, godly toward God — leaving no part of a life over. And the architecture of verse 14 is the whole gospel in order: he gave himself, redeemed, purified, took possession, and the RESULT is a people eager to do good. The works are not the price of the possession; they are what possession produces.

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'For' — and everything changes register. Ten verses of household instruction, and now Paul gives the reason underneath all of it. This is one of the great passages of the New Testament, and it exists to explain why an older woman should not gossip and a slave should not pilfer.

'The grace of God has appeared.' The verb is epiphaino, the shining-out word — used of the sun breaking through, and in that world of a god or a king making a public appearance. Grace was not announced or explained. It showed up, visibly, in a person.

And the tense is past and definite. There was a point in history at which this occurred. Paul is not describing a quality in God's character, though it is that; he is describing an event you could have attended.

'Bringing salvation for all people.' The phrase has been read two ways, and the grammar allows both: grace that brings salvation, appearing to all people; or grace bringing salvation-for-all. Either way the reach is universal in scope — and the immediate context settles what Paul means by it. He has just addressed old men, old women, young women, young men, and slaves. All people, in this chapter, means all kinds of people, and the grace that appeared is not restricted to any tier of society.

That is the answer to a graded religion, and Crete had teachers offering one. On the island of the circumcision party, with its commands of men and its inner knowledge, Paul says the grace of God has appeared to the slave in the kitchen on precisely the same terms as to the master.

Note too the logic of the 'for'. He does not say: behave well, and then grace may appear. He says behave well because it already has. The whole ethical section rests on a completed event, and that order is never reversed anywhere in Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.' The word is paideuo — the raising and schooling of a child, including its discipline. It is the same root as the training in righteousness of 2 Timothy 3:16.

And grace is the subject of the verb. That is the sentence's astonishment. Grace is not merely what pardons the ungodliness; grace is the schoolmaster. The very thing people fear will make men careless is here the thing that trains them out of carelessness.

Anyone who has heard that too much emphasis on grace produces loose living should sit with this verse. Paul's answer is not that grace must be balanced by law. It is that grace itself does the teaching, and does it better, because law can restrain conduct and cannot reach the wanting.

'To renounce' is a decisive word — to deny, to say no to, the same verb used of Peter denying Christ. There is a definite refusal in it rather than a gradual cooling.

Then the positive, and it covers everything: 'to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age.' Three adverbs, and they face three directions. Sophronos — sound-minded, and there is the chapter's word for the fifth time, facing inward toward yourself. Righteously — facing outward toward other people. Godly — facing upward toward God. Between them there is no part of a life left over.

'In the present age.' Not in retreat from it, and not in some future condition when circumstances improve. On Crete, now, among the liars and the lazy gluttons. The grace that appeared in one age trains people to live in another one, and the training is for the age we are actually in.

verseByVerse.quote: waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ.'

The Christian life in this passage stands between two appearings. Grace appeared (v.11); glory will appear (v.13); and between them we live self-controlled lives in the present age. Everything in the chapter sits in that gap.

'Waiting' is not idleness — the word means to look for expectantly, and it is the same posture Paul commended when he said the crown goes to all who have loved his appearing (2 Tim 4:8). And the hope is called blessed, the word for happy, self-sufficiently glad.

Now the crux, and it is one of the most important Christological texts in the New Testament: 'our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ.'

The question is whether Paul is naming one person or two — 'our great God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ', or 'our great God and Saviour, who is Jesus Christ'. The Greek settles it. There is a single definite article governing both nouns, joined by kai, with a personal name attached — the construction described by Granville Sharp, under which two singular personal nouns joined this way refer to the same person. The rule holds consistently in the New Testament, and it holds here.

So Jesus Christ is called, straightforwardly, our great God. It is one of a small handful of places where the New Testament applies the word to him without qualification (cf. John 1:1; 20:28; Rom 9:5; 2 Pet 1:1, which has the identical construction).

And it explains the strange alternation running through this letter. Paul has said God our Saviour and Christ our Saviour, back and forth, six times in three chapters (1:3, 1:4, 2:10, 2:13, 3:4, 3:6). It looked careless. It was an argument being assembled, and here it closes.

Which also lifts the chapter's ordinary instructions into a startling light. The slave not pilfering in a Cretan kitchen is adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v.10) — and the God in question is the man who died for him.

verseByVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Who gave himself for us.' The great God and Saviour of the previous verse is immediately described by a death. Paul does not let the high Christology stand for a sentence without the cross under it.

And the giving is reflexive — he gave himself. Not something of his; not a contribution. The whole person handed over.

Then two purposes, and they are negative and positive. 'To redeem us from all lawlessness' — the verb is the ransom word, to buy out of slavery, which on Crete would be heard by people who had watched it happen in a market. And 'all lawlessness', with nothing left unbought.

'And to purify for himself a people for his own possession.' The language is straight out of the Old Testament — a people for his treasured possession, said of Israel at Sinai (Exod 19:5; Deut 14:2). Paul applies it, without apology, to a scatter of congregations on Crete containing slaves and former liars. What God said of the nation he brought out of Egypt he now says of them.

'Zealous for good works.' The chapter ends where the letter keeps ending. And note the order once more, because it is the whole architecture: he gave himself, he redeemed, he purified, he took possession — and the result is a people eager to do good. The works are not the price of the possession. They are what possession produces.

Then verse 15, and it is aimed squarely at Titus: 'Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority.' All three verbs — announce, encourage, correct — and 'with all authority', which is a command word, the note of someone entitled to speak.

'Let no one disregard you.' The verb means to think around, to look past. Timothy was told not to let anyone despise his youth (1 Tim 4:12); Titus is told not to be ignored. And the instruction is oddly framed — Titus cannot control what people think of him. What he can control is whether he gives them grounds, which is why verses 7-8 told him to be a model whose teaching offers no handle. A man is disregarded either because he has no authority or because he has given it away.

3.title: Heirs of Hope: Conduct in Society and the Gospel's Foundation
3.overview:
The final chapter divides into two movements: the Christian's conduct in civil society (vv. 1–8) and the management of divisive people (vv. 9–15). The first movement is anchored by the most complete soteriological statement in the letter — the 'washing of regeneration' paragraph (vv. 4–7) — which functions as the ground for the preceding practical instructions. Christians submit to civic authorities, avoid slander, pursue gentleness, not because of any native virtue but because of what God has done: he saved us not because of our works but by his own mercy, through the Spirit's renewing, so that we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The ethical instruction makes sense only on this foundation.

Paul includes himself in the 'we were once...' of v. 3 — 'we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures.' This is the kataleptic reminder that grounds Christian gentleness toward the unconverted: we were that. The grace that reached us can reach anyone. The Christian who despises pagan neighbors has forgotten what they themselves were, and what grace found them in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Be Ready for Every Good Work
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The instructions for civic conduct (vv. 1–3) lead into the most complete statement of the gospel's saving work in the entire letter (vv. 4–7). This structure is deliberate: the reason Christians can be gentle, submissive, non-slanderous citizens — even toward a government that may well persecute them — is that they know what they themselves once were, and what God has done. The gospel memory produces the civic virtue. 'Remind them' (v. 1) — the community needs to be reminded of both the practical instruction and its theological foundation. They know both; they need to be kept in them.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 4–7 form one of Paul's great soteriological paragraphs, comparable to Ephesians 2:1–10 in its completeness. Three divine acts are named: (1) God saved us 'not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy' — the exclusion of human merit is categorical. (2) He saved us 'through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit' — the new birth and the Spirit's ongoing renewal as the instruments of salvation. (3) He justified us 'by his grace,' so that 'we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life' — present justification leading to future inheritance. Past, present, and future dimensions of salvation are compressed into four verses. The 'trustworthy saying' formula (v. 8) — the fifth and final occurrence in the Pastorals — marks this as established catechetical teaching, not Pauline novelty.
verseByVerse.examples: The self-inclusion of v. 3 ('we ourselves were once...') is the preacher's most powerful tool for motivating gentleness toward hostile outsiders. A congregation that forgets its own pre-conversion condition becomes contemptuous of unbelievers rather than compassionate toward them. Paul spent years persecuting the church; now he describes his pre-conversion state with unflinching clarity: 'foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.' That is what grace found. That is what grace can still find. Then: Christians in Crete expected to submit to Roman provincial authorities who might well be corrupt or hostile. Now: Christians in democracies tempted to civic contempt and culture-war posturing — the same instruction applies: not political disengagement but the posture of those who know they were once exactly where their opponents are.

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people. For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Submissive to rulers and authorities' (archais exousiais hypotassesthai) — the Pauline political theology of Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2: the Christian is not a revolutionary but a constructive civic presence. This does not require agreeing with every government policy; it does require a default posture of order-respecting cooperation unless obeying the authorities requires disobeying God (Acts 5:29). 'Speak evil of no one' (mēdena blasphēmein) — not to slander anyone, including those in authority; the word is the same as 'blaspheme' when directed toward God, indicating how seriously the New Testament takes verbal harm. 'Avoid quarreling' (amachous einai) — literally: to be non-fighting persons; the compound is striking: not just avoiding quarrels but being the kind of person who is constitutionally non-combative. 'Perfect courtesy toward all people' (epieikian pros pantas anthrōpous) — epieikeia means reasonableness, fairness, the willingness to yield where the strict letter of the law would not require it. 'We ourselves were once...' — the first-person plural is deliberately inclusive of Paul: the apostle refuses to exempt himself from the diagnosis. The grammar of grace that reaches others is the same grammar that reached him. The kataleptic reminder — we were that — is the Christian's ultimate motivation for compassionate engagement rather than contemptuous separation.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Loving kindness' (philanthrōpia) — the love of God for human beings. The word was widely used in Hellenistic royal propaganda to describe the benevolent care of rulers — especially the Roman emperor — for their subjects. Paul takes this imperial claim and attributes it to God against Caesar: the real philanthropy, the real love for humanity, is not found in the palace in Rome but in the appearing of God's mercy in Christ. 'Not because of works done by us in righteousness' — the exclusion of merit is categorical and unqualified; no partial human contribution is left standing. 'Washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit' (loutrou palingenesias kai anakainōseōs pneumatos hagiou) — the most contested soteriological phrase in the letter. Palingenesia (new birth, re-genesis) appears only twice in the NT: here and Matthew 19:28, where it describes the eschatological 'renewal of all things' when the Son of Man sits on his throne. Paul uses the cosmic-renewal word for the individual's new birth: the same creative power that will remake the cosmos has already remade the believer. The 'washing' almost certainly refers to baptism as its primary referent (the early church uniformly read it so), but the debate concerns what the baptism does: Rome and Orthodoxy read dia (through) as indicating baptism regenerates by the act itself (ex opere operato); Calvin and the Reformed tradition read baptism as the sign and seal of regeneration, not its mechanical cause — the Spirit works when and how he will, and baptism is the appointed sign through which the covenant promise is sealed. The phrase 'renewing of the Holy Spirit' ensures that the water alone is never the instrument; the Spirit is always the active agent. 'Poured out on us richly' (execheen eph' hēmas plousiōs) — the Pentecost-of-Joel language (Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18), the abundant gift of the Spirit applied here to every believer in union with Christ. 'Justified by his grace… heirs according to the hope of eternal life' — the three tenses of salvation in one sentence: regeneration (past), justification (present standing), inheritance (future expectation). 'The saying is trustworthy' (pistos ho logos) — the fifth and final occurrence of the formula in the Pastorals, marking this soteriological paragraph as received catechetical teaching, the church's confessional anchor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter ends with practical instruction about managing divisive people and supporting mobile ministers. The contrast with vv. 4–8 is sharp: the great soteriological paragraph gives way to 'avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law.' The point of the juxtaposition is not accidental: having stated what is truly profitable (v. 8), Paul immediately names what is not. The diagnostic test for any ministerial controversy is v. 9: 'they are unprofitable and worthless.' If a debate produces no spiritual benefit for the participants, it should be dropped.
verseByVerse.theology: 'A person who stirs up division' (hairetikon anthrōpon) — the word hairetikos is the ancestor of the English 'heretic,' but in New Testament usage it does not yet carry the full doctrinal-error sense it will later acquire. Hairesis means a choice, a sect, a party; a hairetikos person is one who creates factions by drawing people to himself or to a party, dividing the community. The primary crime is divisiveness, not necessarily theological error (though error typically accompanies it). The two-warning discipline (v. 10 — 'after warning him once and then twice') echoes Matthew 18:15–17's escalating confrontation pattern. After two warnings, separation — not because reconciliation is impossible to God, but because the community cannot afford indefinite disruption, and the person has made his choice: 'he is self-condemned' (autokatakritos).
verseByVerse.examples: The 'two warnings then separate' discipline is the most commonly neglected piece of pastoral practice in Titus. Churches tolerate divisive individuals for years out of misplaced mercy — a mercy that is in fact no mercy to the congregation being disrupted or to the divisive person who is never made to feel the weight of what they are doing. Paul's instruction is not harsh; it is the most realistic form of compassion available: confront clearly, twice, then release them to the consequences of their own choice. 'Self-condemned' is a pastoral observation: the person who persists after two clear warnings has condemned himself; the church is not condemning him. Then: Cretan teachers generating factions over Jewish genealogical speculation. Now: online-driven theological controversy that generates heat without illumination, fracturing congregations over secondary issues — same category, same remedy.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinning; he is self-condemned. When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful. All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law' — the four terms all belong to the Jewish speculative tradition that was disrupting the Cretan churches: elaborate midrashic debates over genealogical tables, halakhic disputes over Torah interpretation. 'Unprofitable and worthless' (anōpheleis kai mataioi) — the two-word verdict is the letter's practical diagnostic: does this debate benefit anyone? If not, stop. 'A person who stirs up division' (hairetikon anthrōpon) — from hairesis (choice, sect; the word group from which 'heretic' derives). In New Testament usage, a hairetikos is primarily a party-former, a community-divider, not yet the later technical sense of doctrinal heretic — though false doctrine typically accompanies the divisive behavior. 'Self-condemned' (autokatakritos) — a compound found only here in Greek literature; the person who persists after two explicit warnings has issued the verdict against himself; the church is merely recognizing what he has declared. 'Artemas or Tychicus' — Paul plans to send one of them to relieve Titus so Titus can join him at Nicopolis (on the Adriatic, in Epirus — a significant western base for further mission work). 'Zenas the lawyer and Apollos' — Zenas is otherwise unknown; his title (nomikos) may indicate a Roman lawyer or a Jewish Torah-expert. Apollos is the Alexandrian rhetorician of Acts 18, trained by Priscilla and Aquila; he is traveling with Zenas. The instruction to 'see that they lack nothing' — the local church is expected to provide material support for traveling ministers; hospitality and financial provision are themselves forms of participation in the mission. 'Let our people devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need' — the letter's final practical instruction returns to its dominant theme: the gospel-shaped community is known by its practical goodness, its willingness to meet real need, its refusal to be spiritually unfruitful.
